facts.subject: voice
facts.content: Terse, precise, engineer-to-engineer — Electron writes the way a good commit message reads: exactly what changed, why, nothing extra. No marketing adjectives; a feature is described by what it does and what it costs (bundle size, latency, breaking changes), never by how exciting it is. Code samples are the default form of proof, not screenshots or claims. Passive voice is avoided in favor of a stated actor ('the scheduler retries the job', not 'the job gets retried'). Never uses exclamation points. Documentation-register sentences are preferred over conversational ones even in social copy — the brand would rather be slightly dry than slightly imprecise.

facts.subject: tone
facts.content: By surface: release notes are exhaustive and neutral (every breaking change gets its own line with a migration note, no editorializing about how great the release is); docs are patient but assume competence (define jargon once, then use it freely); RFC/design-doc posts show tradeoffs explicitly, including the rejected alternatives and why; social/launch posts are still understated — a major feature launch gets one calm paragraph and a code snippet, not a countdown or hype thread. Bugs and incidents are addressed head-on in public postmortems with a timeline and root cause, never buried or softened.

facts.subject: instincts
facts.content: Every performance or capability claim needs a benchmark, a reproducible repro, or a linked PR — an unverified claim doesn't ship, full stop. Breaking changes always get a deprecation window and a codemod or migration guide when feasible; 'just update your code' is never acceptable messaging on its own. Security disclosures follow coordinated disclosure — nothing about an unpatched vulnerability goes public before a fix is released, even internally-facing drafts. When comparing to competing tools, cite specific measured differences (bundle size, cold-start time, API surface) rather than general superiority language. Contributor-facing content credits the specific person/PR by name; never anonymize community contributions into 'the team'.

facts.subject: banned_words
facts.content: revolutionary, game-changing, blazing fast, best-in-class, industry-leading, seamless, effortless, magic, just works, 10x, disrupt

lessons.subject: unbenchmarked performance claims get corrected publicly by maintainers
lessons.content: An early launch post claimed a rewrite was 'significantly faster' without a benchmark attached; a maintainer posted an independent benchmark showing mixed results within the day, forcing a public correction. Every performance claim now ships with a linked, reproducible benchmark in the same post, not a follow-up.

lessons.subject: breaking changes without a migration path stall adoption
lessons.content: A major version bump that changed a core API with only a changelog line (no codemod, no migration guide) saw adoption stall for weeks — issues filled up with people asking how to upgrade. Any breaking API change now ships with either a codemod or a step-by-step migration guide in the same release, not as a follow-up doc.

lessons.subject: silent security fixes erode trust more than public disclosures
lessons.content: A patch that quietly fixed a security issue without an accompanying advisory was later flagged by a community member who diffed the release, and the resulting 'why wasn't this disclosed' thread did more reputational damage than a straightforward disclosure would have. Every security-relevant fix now gets a formal advisory with severity, affected versions, and fix version, published alongside the release.

lessons.subject: over-explaining basics in docs slows down the target audience
lessons.content: Early documentation drafts explained fundamental concepts (what an event loop is, what a promise is) at length, and experienced-developer feedback consistently said the docs felt padded and hard to skim. Docs now define jargon once with a link out to prior art, then move directly into the specific behavior — the audience is assumed competent.

lessons.subject: unattributed contributor work reads as erasure, not humility
lessons.content: A recap post that credited a major feature to 'the team' rather than the external contributor who wrote it drew a public correction request from that contributor. Release notes and recap posts now name the specific contributor and link their PR/profile for any community-authored work.

general_facts.subject: key people
general_facts.content: Marcus Webb is the maintainer lead who writes most release notes and RFCs; he has final say on breaking-change timing. Aiko Tanaka runs security disclosures and coordinates the advisory process for any vulnerability fix.

general_facts.subject: core audience
general_facts.content: Primarily professional software engineers evaluating or already using the tool in production; a secondary audience is open-source contributors following the project's RFC and design-doc process.

general_facts.subject: flagship content series
general_facts.content: The 'RFC Deep Dive' series walks through a design doc's tradeoffs and rejected alternatives after a feature ships; it's the highest-engagement recurring format among the technical audience and is the tone benchmark for design-doc-style posts.

general_facts.subject: release cadence
general_facts.content: Minor releases ship every two weeks on a fixed Tuesday cadence; major (breaking) releases ship at most twice a year and always include a deprecation window of at least one full minor-release cycle before removal.

general_facts.subject: standing preference
general_facts.content: The project does not do paid placements or sponsored feature coverage of any kind — this is a hard line stated explicitly in the contributor guidelines, not just an informal norm, after early inbound sponsorship offers were publicly declined to preserve neutrality.
